podcast.title: Founding as Record Store (1976)
podcast.body: In 1976, Jeff Travis founded Rough Trade as a record store in Notting Hill, London. He started it with his personal record collection after a trip across the US where he bought many records. The store quickly became a hub for non-mainstream music enthusiasts. "In 1976, Jeff Travis took a trip across the US buying up all kinds of records and when he got home he didn't have anywhere to put them so he decided to start up a store with his record collection acting as inventory."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 1

podcast.title: Formation (1978)
podcast.body: Rough Trade was one of three important independent labels, alongside Factory Records and Mute Records, that began releasing material in 1978. These labels emerged with non-commercial aims after the punk revolution opened doors for riskier music. "rap, rate... empezaron a literar material en ese mismo año 1978."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: La traición que salvó al punk. PiL

podcast.title: Transition to Record Label (1978)
podcast.body: In 1978, Jeff Travis expanded Rough Trade into an independent record label. One of its earliest releases was "Alternative Ulster" by the Belfast band Stiff Little Fingers. "In 1978, Travis decided to jump into the indie record label game and one of the labels very earliest releases was by a bell fast band called Stiff Little Fingers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 1

podcast.title: The Strokes' "The Modern Age" EP (2001)
podcast.body: Rough Trade Records in the UK agreed to release The Strokes' *The Modern Age* EP on January 29, 2001, after US labels showed no interest. The EP's immense demand led to the label struggling to maintain supply to shops. "they sent a demo to rough trade records in the UK, who agreed to release an EP called The Modern Age. When it came out on January 29, 2001, rough trade struggled to maintain a supply to the shops."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: History of Indie Rock: Part 4

podcast.title: British Independent (Indy) Label
podcast.body: Rough Trade was listed as an example of a British independent label, consistently referred to as "Indy" in the UK. These labels maintained their autonomy, operating entirely separately from the dominant major multinational record labels of the period. "And this list included mute and factory and rough trade and creation and dozens more."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Etymology: Part 1

podcast.title: British Indie Label Influence
podcast.body: A London-based independent record label known for its significant role in breaking new music, particularly since the punk era in the 1970s. They provided an early platform for bands like The Strokes. "The strokes started by sending a demo to Rough Trade Records in London, and they agreed to release an EP called The Modern Age."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 00's Part 2: The Indie Revolution

podcast.title: Community Hub
podcast.body: The Rough Trade store served as a community gathering place where people bought records, promoted fanzines, exchanged gossip, and advertised for musicians. The original shop remains open near Portobello Road in Notting Hill. "It also became a hangout for people into non-mainstream music. They bought records, they pushed fanzines, they swapped gossip and advertised for musicians."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 1

podcast.title: Dominant British Independent Label
podcast.body: Rough Trade is identified as one of the independent labels that dominate much of the British rock scene today. "much of the British rock scene is dominated by independent labels like Domino and Cooking Vinyl and Go Disks, Rough Trade, XL Recording and dozens and dozens more."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rock Snob

podcast.title: Early Supporter of DIY Electronic Music
podcast.body: Rough Trade record shop in Notting Hill played a crucial role in the early Technopop scene by agreeing to stock Daniel Miller's self-produced "Warm Leatherette" single, which was recorded with rudimentary gear in his bedroom. This support helped the minimalist, futuristic record sell 30,000 copies, inspiring many aspiring musicians. "He started experimenting with it in his bedroom. Recorded two songs, found some money to make a test pressing and convinced the rough-trade record shop in Notting Hill to stock it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 2: Techno-Pop

podcast.title: Financial Struggles and Bankruptcy
podcast.body: While Rough Trade found success with acts like The Smiths, most of its early signings sold records "by the dozen." The label eventually faced financial difficulties and went bankrupt by 1991, impacting other independent labels with which it had existing arrangements. "rough trade went bankrupt by 1991 and by then they had arrangements with other indie labels and they were all hurt as a result."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 9

podcast.title: Founding and Evolution
podcast.body: Rough Trade was founded by Geoff Travis, initially as a record shop in London in 1976, which he opened to sell his extensive record collection accumulated in Canada and the United States. By 1978, the shop had expanded into a record label focused on finding new and exciting post-punk bands. "It started when he had this giant record collection that he needed to sell off."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 9

podcast.title: Home to The Smiths
podcast.body: Rough Trade served as the UK home label for The Smiths, widely considered the biggest indie band of their era and one whose influences continue to be discussed. "As this tape was getting people excited about the possibilities of new music, rough trade was home to the biggest indie band of the era, whose influences are still being talked about today."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 2

podcast.title: London Store Experience
podcast.body: The speaker purchased their first White Stripes record, *White Blood Cells*, at the original Rough Trade store in Notting Hill, London, highlighting the label's physical presence and influence in the indie music scene. "I bought my first white stripes record at the original Rough Trade store in Notting Hill, London."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: History of Indie Rock: Part 4

podcast.title: Maintaining Physical Locations
podcast.body: Rough Trade Records was highlighted as one of the few music retailers that continued to operate multiple physical locations, with two in London, one in Bristol, one in Nottingham, one in Liverpool, and two in New York, contrasting with the general mass extinction of chain stores. "They have two locations in London, one in Bristol, another in Nottingham, one in Liverpool, and a couple of New York locations."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pioneering Independent Label
podcast.body: Rough Trade was among the small independent labels that emerged in the post-punk era, specializing in operating outside the major label system and supporting independent artists. "that included rough trade for a D, beggars banquet, epitaph, SST, and many others."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 7: All the rest

podcast.title: Prominent on C86 Cassette
podcast.body: Rough Trade was one of the indie labels whose artists were tapped to be featured on the influential C86 cassette, a compilation that reflected the state of new music in Britain in 1986. "They tapped labels like Creation and Rough Tray and a bunch of others."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 2

podcast.title: Recommended Record Store in London
podcast.body: Rough Trade is recommended as a must-visit record store in London, with specific locations mentioned in Notting Hill and the East End store in Brick Lane. "I never go to London without visiting Rough Trade and Notting Hill or the East End store in Brick Lane."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the Record Store

podcast.title: Resurrection for The Strokes
podcast.body: Rough Trade Records (UK) won a fierce bidding war for The Strokes after the success of their "The Modern Age" EP. At the time, the company had ceased operating as a label and was only managing bands. However, company head Geoff Travis was so impressed with The Strokes that he resurrected the label specifically to sign and release their music. "The winner in the bidding war was UK's Rough Trade Records, even though they'd stopped being a label at the time and were only managing bands."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Strokes

podcast.title: Signed The Strokes
podcast.body: Rough Trade, a UK-based label, signed The Strokes after American labels showed no interest in the band despite the buzz they had generated. Rough Trade "loved what they heard" from the band's demos, leading to their debut album "This Is It." "So they sent some demos to Rough Trade in the UK, and Rough Trade loved what they heard."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 4: Garage Rock

podcast.title: The Smiths' Record Company
podcast.body: Rough Trade was the record company for The Smiths, but the relationship was fraught with "big, big problems." These issues worsened after the release of "The Queen Is Dead" and were even satirized in The Smiths' song "Frankly, Mr. Shankly," where "Mr. Shankly" referred to label head Jeff Travis. "And there were big, big problems with rough trade, the Smiths record company."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About The Smiths

podcast.title: The Sundays' Deal and Financial Difficulties
podcast.body: The Sundays secured a record deal with Rough Trade Records. The label later encountered financial difficulties, which led The Sundays to take over management of their own affairs. "they got a deal with rough trade records. When rough trade ran into financial difficulties, they started managing everything themselves"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: UK Distribution Deal for Funeral
podcast.body: Rough Trade Records secured a distribution deal for Arcade Fire's *Funeral* album in the UK, playing a crucial role in the band's initial recognition and success across the Atlantic. "thanks to a distribution deal with rough trade records."
